title: Weathering and Erosion
seo_title: Grade 4 Science: Weathering and Erosion Worksheets (Ontario Curriculum)
standard_text: Describe how weathering and erosion by water, wind, ice and living things change the land; identify slow and fast changes to landforms; assess ways to reduce erosion. (summary of the Ontario Science and Technology curriculum, 2022, Strand E: Earth and Space Systems – Rocks, Minerals, and Erosion)
meta_desc: Free Grade 4 science worksheets on weathering, erosion, deposition, freeze-thaw, glaciers and protecting land in Ontario. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: Weathering breaks rock; erosion moves it.
key_sub: Water, wind, ice and living things shape the land, slowly or quickly.
body_html:
How to think about it

Weathering breaks rocks into smaller pieces. Erosion carries the pieces away. Deposition drops them somewhere new.

  • Water freezing in cracks breaks rock (freeze-thaw), which is common in Ontario winters.
  • Plant roots and burrowing animals also break rock and soil.
  • Glaciers carved the Great Lakes; rivers, waves and wind keep shaping the land.
  • Plants, windbreaks and retaining walls help stop soil erosion.
Example

Water freezes in a crack in a rock. What happens?

ice takes up more space

Answer: the rock breaks

Example

Is a landslide a fast or slow change?

it happens in seconds

Answer: fast

Common mistakes

  • Mixing up weathering (breaking) and erosion (moving).
  • Thinking erosion only happens by water.
  • Thinking land never changes.

faq.q: What is the difference between weathering and erosion?
faq.a: Weathering breaks rock down. Erosion moves the broken pieces to a new place.
Thick ice sheets scraped the land, carved valleys and lake basins and left behind rocks and sand when they melted.

faq.q: How can we stop soil erosion?
faq.a: By planting trees and grass, building windbreaks and walls, and not removing plants from slopes.

items.q: A muddy river carries soil many kilometres downstream. Which process is this?
items.e: Transportation carries the pieces to a new place.

items.q: Heavy rain washes soil off a bare hillside. Which process is this?
items.e: Erosion picks up and removes rock pieces and soil.

items.q: Salt crystals grow in tiny holes in a sea cliff and crumble the sandstone. Which process is this?
items.e: Weathering breaks rock into smaller pieces where it is.

items.q: Sand settles on the inside bend of a river where the water is slow. Which process is this?
items.e: Deposition drops the pieces when the water, wind or ice slows down.

items.q: Lichen growing on a rock slowly breaks down its surface. Which process is this?
items.e: Weathering breaks rock into smaller pieces where it is.

items.q: Strong wind picks up loose sand from a dune. Which process is this?
items.e: Erosion picks up and removes rock pieces and soil.

items.q: What is deposition?
c: dropping eroded sediment in a new place
items.e: Rivers drop sand where they slow down.

items.q: Which change happens very quickly?
c: a glacier wearing down a mountain
items.e: Some changes take seconds, others take millions of years.

items.q: Water seeps into a crack in a rock, freezes, expands and splits the rock. Which process is this?
items.e: Weathering breaks rock into smaller pieces where it is.

items.q: Why do farmers plant rows of trees between fields?
c: to slow the wind and reduce soil erosion
items.e: Windbreaks protect soil.

items.q: Benjamin finds a photo of a town flooded the day after a big storm. Is this evidence of a fast change or a slow change?
items.e: It happened in one day.

items.q: Niagara Falls moves slowly back upstream over time. Why?
c: The falls are pushed by wind.
Water erodes the soft rock under the hard top layer.
items.e: Erosion changes landforms.

items.q: How did the Great Lakes form?
c: Huge glaciers carved out the land, then melted.
items.e: Ice is a powerful agent of erosion.

items.q: Chloe finds photos of a cliff taken 50 years apart that look almost the same. Is this evidence of a fast change or a slow change?
items.e: The cliff barely changed in 50 years.

items.q: Why do pebbles in a river become round?
c: They knock against each other and wear away their sharp edges.
items.e: This happens as they are transported.

items.q: What is a glacier?
c: a huge, slow-moving body of ice
items.e: Glaciers erode the land as they move.

items.q: Which change happens fastest?
items.e: Some changes take minutes; others take thousands of years.

items.q: What can farmers plant to reduce wind erosion?
items.e: Windbreaks slow the wind.

items.q: Which change is usually slowest?
c: a storm washing away a beach
items.e: Weathering by wind can take thousands of years.

items.q: Cattle trample a riverbank and the soil is washed away. Which process is this?
items.e: Erosion picks up and removes rock pieces and soil.

items.q: A cliff is changed by weathering, erosion, transportation and deposition. Which step usually comes third?
items.e: The usual order: weathering, erosion, transportation, deposition.

items.q: Frozen water in alpine cracks splits rocks into sharp pieces. What is mainly causing this change?
items.e: The cause of this change is ice.

items.q: Why are retaining walls built on steep slopes?
c: to hold soil and rock in place
items.e: Walls reduce landslides.

items.q: A desert rock is shaped like a mushroom by sand blowing near the ground. What is mainly causing this change?
items.e: The cause of this change is wind.

items.q: Which process mainly formed the mouth of the Murray River?
c: weathering and erosion by wind and rain
items.e: The river slows and drops sand and mud where it meets the sea.

items.q: A cliff is changed by weathering, erosion, transportation and deposition. Which step usually comes second?
items.e: The usual order: weathering, erosion, transportation, deposition.

items.q: What is erosion?
c: the moving of soil and rock pieces by water, wind or ice
the breaking of rock in place only
items.e: Erosion carries sediment away.

items.q: Sand blasts against a rock in a dust storm and smooths it. What is mainly causing this change?
items.e: The cause of this change is wind.

items.q: Which process mainly formed Kings Canyon in the Northern Territory?
c: weathering and erosion by wind and rain
items.e: Water and weathering cut deep into the sandstone.

items.q: A creek carves a deep gorge in the hills over thousands of years. What is mainly causing this change?
items.e: The cause of this change is running water.

items.q: Why do rocks in a fast river become smooth and round?
c: They bump and rub against each other as the water carries them.
items.e: Moving water erodes rock.

items.q: A huge chunk of a cliff collapses onto the beach below. What is mainly causing this change?
items.e: The cause of this change is gravity.

items.q: Which process mainly formed the Twelve Apostles in Victoria?
items.e: Waves eroded the limestone cliffs, leaving stacks of rock.

items.q: Which process mainly formed the sand dunes of K'gari (Fraser Island)?
c: weathering and erosion by wind and rain
items.e: Wind and waves dropped huge amounts of sand.

items.q: Sand dunes slowly move inland across the coast. What is mainly causing this change?
items.e: The cause of this change is wind.

items.q: Why do potholes appear on Ontario roads in spring?
c: Water freezes and thaws in cracks, breaking the road.
Rain is acidic only in spring.
items.e: Freeze-thaw weathering breaks up roads.

items.q: A flood washes a gully into a paddock. What is mainly causing this change?
items.e: The cause of this change is running water.

items.q: A cliff is changed by weathering, erosion, transportation and deposition. Which step usually comes first?
items.e: The usual order: weathering, erosion, transportation, deposition.

items.q: Where does a river drop most of its sediment?
c: where it slows down, like at its mouth
at the top of a waterfall
items.e: Slow water cannot carry as much.

items.q: Boulders tumble down a gorge wall and pile up at the bottom. What is mainly causing this change?
items.e: The cause of this change is gravity.

items.q: Hana compares a storm wave hitting a dune and a cave forming. Which happens faster?
c: a storm wave hitting a dune
items.e: A storm wave hitting a dune takes hours; a cave forming takes thousands of years.

items.q: Emma reads: “A glacier slides down a valley and shapes it.” Is this a fast change or a slow change?
c: It happens every day in every town.
items.e: It takes thousands of years, so it is slow.

items.q: Which change to the land takes the longest?
c: a river carving a deep valley
items.e: River valleys form over thousands of years.

items.q: Jayden reads: “A big storm wave knocks down part of a sand dune.” How long does this usually take?
items.e: This is a fast change: hours.

items.q: Which agent of erosion shaped the sand dunes at Sandbanks Provincial Park?
items.e: Wind moves sand into dunes.

items.q: Liam reads: “A river carves a deep canyon.” Is this a fast change or a slow change?
c: It happens every day in every town.
items.e: It takes millions of years, so it is slow.

items.q: Ava compares a rock falling off a cliff and roots cracking a rock. Which happens faster?
c: a rock falling off a cliff
items.e: A rock falling off a cliff takes seconds; roots cracking a rock takes many years.

items.q: A farmer leaves bare soil all winter. What can happen in spring?
c: Melting snow and rain wash the soil away.
items.e: Cover crops protect soil.

items.q: Leah compares a storm wave hitting a dune and mud turning into rock. Which happens faster?
c: a storm wave hitting a dune
items.e: A storm wave hitting a dune takes hours; mud turning into rock takes millions of years.

items.q: What is weathering?
c: dropping sediment in a new place
the breaking down of rock into smaller pieces
items.e: Weathering breaks; erosion moves.

items.q: Zoe looks at this picture. This storm floods a town. Is it a fast change or a slow change?
items.e: It takes hours or days.

items.q: Aiden reads: “An earthquake shakes the ground and cracks a road.” Is this a fast change or a slow change?
c: It happens every day in every town.
items.e: It takes seconds or minutes, so it is fast.

items.q: Ethan compares a landslide and mud turning into rock. Which happens slower?
items.e: Mud turning into rock takes millions of years; a landslide takes minutes.

items.q: Noah looks at this picture. A river carved this canyon. How long does it take?
items.e: It is a slow change.

items.q: Owen looks at this picture. This volcano erupts. Is it a fast change or a slow change?
items.e: It takes hours or days.

items.q: Emma reads: “A rock falls off a cliff.” How long does this usually take?
items.e: This is a fast change: seconds.

items.q: Mei reads: “Tree roots crack a big rock.” Is this a fast change or a slow change?
c: It happens every day in every town.
items.e: It takes many years, so it is slow.

items.q: Nathan reads: “A flood fills a town's streets with water.” Is this a fast change or a slow change?
c: It happens every day in every town.
items.e: It takes hours or days, so it is fast.

items.q: Ethan looks at this picture. This volcano erupts. How long does it take?
items.e: It is a fast change.

items.q: Ethan looks at this picture. A river carved this canyon. Is it a fast change or a slow change?
items.e: It takes millions of years.

items.q: How long can a big canyon take to form?
items.e: Rivers cut rock very slowly.

items.q: Can a slow change still change the land a lot?
c: Yes, over a very long time.
items.e: Slow does not mean small.

items.q: What does 'weathering' mean?
c: rock slowly breaking into smaller pieces
items.e: Wind, water and ice break rock.

items.q: Chloe finds a book that says the canyon took millions of years to form. Is this evidence of a fast change or a slow change?
items.e: Millions of years is very slow.

items.q: Hana finds a chart showing a beach losing a little sand each year for 100 years. Is this evidence of a fast change or a slow change?
items.e: A little each year for 100 years.

items.q: Chloe pours 500 mL of water on two trays of soil. One is bare; one has grass. The bare tray loses 120 g of soil. Which result is most likely for the grass tray?
items.e: Grass roots hold the soil.

items.q: A stream table has water flowing on a gentle slope. Where will most sand be dropped?
c: in the middle of the fastest part
at the top, where the water starts
at the bottom, where the water spreads out and slows
items.e: Slow water deposits sand.

items.q: Ocean waves crash against a rocky shore. What happens to the rocks over time?
c: They are broken and smoothed into pebbles and sand.
items.e: Waves are an agent of erosion.

items.q: A beach lost 3 m of sand in a big storm. Over the next 6 months it gained 1 m back each 2 months. How wide is it now compared with before the storm?
items.e: Erosion in the storm, deposition afterwards: 1 m × 3 = 3 m.

items.q: Emma finds a video of mud sliding over a road in 1 minute. Is this evidence of a fast change or a slow change?
items.e: It happened in 1 minute.

items.q: In a stream table, which change would carry the most sand away?
c: the same slope and no water
a steeper slope and more water
a flatter slope and less water
items.e: Faster water erodes and carries more.

items.q: Noah finds an old photo of a big rock and a new photo of the same rock, only a bit smaller after 100 years. Is this evidence of a fast change or a slow change?
items.e: It took 100 years to change a little.

items.q: What does 'erosion' mean?
c: wind or water carrying rock and soil away
items.e: Bits are moved to new places.

items.q: Which change is fast?
items.e: Earthquakes last seconds or minutes.

items.q: What can a volcano do in a few hours?
items.e: Eruptions are fast.

items.q: Ethan says, 'Weathering and erosion are the same thing.' Which reply is best?
c: Weathering breaks rock; erosion moves the pieces away.
Erosion breaks rock; weathering moves it.
items.e: One breaks, the other moves.

items.q: Where can you find out about Earth changes?
items.e: Use more than one source.

items.q: Zoe puts sugar cubes in a jar and shakes it for 2 minutes, then 4, then 6. The cubes get smaller each time. What does this model?
c: rocks being worn down as they knock together
items.e: Shaking models rocks rolling in a river.

items.q: Kai blows through a straw at a pile of sand and gravel. What does he see?
c: The fine sand moves further than the gravel.
The gravel moves further than the sand.
items.e: Wind can carry light pieces further.

items.q: Hana photographs a creek bank every month for a year. The bank moves back 40 cm. Which question does this answer?
c: How fast is the creek eroding its bank?
What will the weather be tomorrow?
How many fish live in the creek?
items.e: Repeated photos measure slow change.

items.q: Which of these is caused by deposition?
c: a cliff falling into the sea
a sandbar at the mouth of a creek
items.e: A sandbar forms where sand is dropped.

items.q: Water seeps into a crack in a rock and freezes. What happens?
c: The ice expands and breaks the rock (freeze-thaw).
items.e: Ontario winters cause a lot of freeze-thaw weathering.

items.q: A river carries mud out to sea after heavy rain. What is mainly causing this change?
items.e: The cause of this change is running water.

items.q: Ocean swell slowly wears down a rock platform. What is mainly causing this change?
items.e: The cause of this change is waves.

items.q: Kai wants evidence that a beach is wearing away. Which source helps most?
c: photos of the beach taken every year for 20 years
items.e: Photos over time show slow change.

items.q: Which word means dropping sand, mud or pebbles in a new place?
items.e: Deposition happens when the moving water or wind slows down.

items.q: A tree root grows into a crack and slowly pushes the rock apart. Which process is this?
items.e: Weathering breaks rock into smaller pieces where it is.

items.q: A fast creek scrapes sand and pebbles from its banks. Which process is this?
items.e: Erosion picks up and removes rock pieces and soil.

items.q: A river bank is wearing away near a farm. Which solution would help most?
c: plant shrubs and trees along the bank
remove the plants on the bank
items.e: Roots hold soil.

items.q: Which word means rock breaking into smaller pieces without being moved?
items.e: Weathering happens in place.

items.q: A glacier moves 1 foot each day. How far does it move in 7 days?
items.e: 7 × 1 = 7. Still slow!

items.q: A river slows down where it meets the sea and drops mud, forming new land. Which process is this?
items.e: Deposition drops the pieces when the water, wind or ice slows down.

items.q: Emma reads that a landslide covered a road in 2 minutes. Which word fits?
items.e: 2 minutes is fast.

items.q: Fine sand is blown off a ploughed field on a windy day. What is mainly causing this change?
items.e: The cause of this change is wind.

items.q: Rainwater slowly dissolves limestone and makes a cave. Which process is this?
items.e: Weathering breaks rock into smaller pieces where it is.

items.q: Where does a river drop most of its sand and mud?
c: at the fastest part of the river
at the top of a waterfall
where it slows down, such as at its mouth
items.e: Slow water cannot carry as much.

items.q: Liam says the Grand Canyon formed in one big flood. Is he right?
c: No. A river carved it over millions of years.
items.e: Canyons form slowly.

items.q: Ava's photo from 1950 and her photo from today show the same cliff, almost the same. What kind of change is the cliff having?
items.e: Very little change in many years.

items.q: Why does bare soil erode more than soil covered by grass?
c: Roots hold the soil and leaves slow the rain.
items.e: Plants protect soil.

items.q: On Kosciuszko, freezing nights crack rocks on the mountain top. What is mainly causing this change?
items.e: The cause of this change is ice.
